posts.text:
AI is not a level playing field.

Nor do I think we should assume it was ever going to democratise opportunity equally for everyone.

We're seeing this increasingly.

There's simply too much at stake. Billions—nay, trillions—and that's probably just the beginning.

And it isn't merely a race between companies anymore.

It's political.

Artificial intelligence—or, if we eventually get there, superintelligence—is becoming the new arms race. Compute. Chips. Models. Energy. Talent. Data. Infrastructure.

Enough apparently to inspire stories involving honeypot spies.

But let's move on. 😂

I've argued before that it would be naive to assume AI will automatically enrich the lives of people in less developed countries simply because the technology exists.

I'm beginning to wonder whether we should apply the same scepticism to open-weight AI, because there is an uncomfortable tension here.

AI can democratise capability. A small company in Singapore can suddenly build things that once required enormous engineering teams. A developer somewhere in Vietnam, India, Indonesia or Africa can gain access to capabilities previously concentrated inside the world's largest technology companies.

But democratising capability doesn't necessarily democratise power.

In fact, the more capable open models become, the more they potentially threaten organisations—and countries—whose advantage depends partly on controlling access to the best intelligence.

So what does that mean for the rest of us?

I don't think the answer is to wait for AI to become a level playing field.

It probably won't.

The countries, companies and individuals who benefit most may be those who recognise that early and build as much capability, knowledge and independence as they can while the window remains open.

Use the APIs. Learn from the frontier models. Use open weights where they make sense. Build local capability. Develop your own people. Own more of your operational knowledge.

Because the biggest divide created by AI may eventually be less about who has access to AI.

Almost everyone probably will.

It may be between those who merely consume intelligence and those who develop the capability tobuild with it, adapt it and control how they use it.

And that is a very different kind of digital divide.

One loan. Fourteen sites. Five countries.
In September 2024, two lenders agreed a US$30 million green loan for BECIS Bioenergy. An accordion could add US$20 million. The total would reach US$50 million.

The loan supports 14 bioenergy installations. They are in Indonesia, Thailand, Cambodia, the Philippines and India. They turn agricultural waste into steam. The steam is sold to commercial and industrial customers under long-term offtake agreements.

Small units look risky one by one. Repeated across a portfolio on one contract type, they can become one credit story.

The public sources give no tenor, no pricing and no per-site capacity. So we draw no conclusion on terms.

What the deal shows is the logic. A repeatable offtake contract can matter more than the size of one site.

For a developer with several small projects, the question is simple. Could your sites be financed together, on one contract template?

We structure this in our Project Finance path. Book a discovery call to test your portfolio.

Exactly two years ago today. November 19, 2024. A day worth remembering.

That was the day the Ministry of Public Works held the closing ceremony of the National Urban Water Supply Project (NUWSP), a journey that began in August 2018.

And what a journey it was!

NUWSP didn't have a smooth start. We struggled, faced delays, and at one point the project was even rated "At Risk". But through persistence and teamwork, we turned things around.

By closing, the project had helped improve water access for over 8.4 million people, strengthened local governments and water utilities, and achieved a satisfactory rating in its ICR. The icing on the cake? Our task team received a World Bank VPU Team Award in 2025.

And let's not forget COVID! 

For almost two years, we practically worked from home. Endless virtual meetings, remote reviews, disrupted field visits, and constant follow-ups. Keeping the project moving wasn't easy, but somehow we made it work.

Yet, looking back, the numbers and awards aren't what I remember most.

I remember the people.

A special thank you to Irma Setiono, who trusted me to join the task team despite my not being a water engineer, not went to ITB's Environmental Engineering program, and knowing practically nothing about the sector. I learned so much from colleagues, many far more senior than me, who always made me feel part of the team.

Countless meetings. Countless discussions. Countless field visits. Countless documents to review (and review again!). Along the way, I learned that development work is as much about people and trust as technical solutions.

And then there was Kemendagri, our Ministry of Home Affairs counterpart! 😄

From occasionally getting on each other's nerves over No Objection Letters to eventually knowing almost everyone in the CPIU team, not just as counterparts, but as friends and practically family. Those relationships are something I'll always treasure.

My sincere appreciation also goes to Maria Angelica Sotomayor, probably the sweetest manager one could ask for. Thank you for your patience, guidance, and encouragement.

To everyone in the task team, our government counterparts, consultants, and colleagues across the country, thank you for making this journey memorable.

Projects close. Reports get archived. Teams move on. But the friendships, lessons, and memories stay.

Two years later, I'm still grateful to have been part of this journey.

Who owns the know-how after the visiting engineers leave?

For manufacturers entering or expanding in Indonesia, technology transfer is also a recruitment decision.

Language fluency helps teams communicate. It does not, by itself, demonstrate process ownership, quality judgment or the ability to train others.

Before recruiting your Indonesia team, align Operations and HR around three questions:
Ownership: Which process, quality decision or training outcome will this person own?
Evidence: What comparable experience shows they can absorb, apply and explain new methods?
Readiness: How will you assess whether the team can perform after the handover?
Turn those answers into role requirements—not just a list of qualifications.

For engineering, quality and production leadership roles, use structured interviews and fictional work scenarios. Ask candidates how they would diagnose a process issue, document learning and validate team readiness. Avoid requesting confidential materials from previous employers.

Map the talent early. Align hiring dates with approved project milestones.

In 2022 my job was getting releases out. In 2025 part of my job was showing a bank's change management process that a release was ready to go out.

Between those two dates I was a release engineer at Vascomm from June 2022, ran a small software house from July 2023, and from January 2025 worked on-site as a DevOps engineer at Bank Syariah Indonesia, building CI/CD on OpenShift.

At the bank, a release did not move on a green pipeline alone. The automated security checks had to pass before production, and the approval step needed deployment evidence that someone could read without an engineer beside them.

Since then I ask three questions of any release:

1. What exactly was deployed?
2. Which checks ran against it, and did they pass?
3. Who approved it, and when?

That is why I am now looking at technology risk and IT audit roles. The pipeline was the part I built. The evidence was the part other people relied on.

POWER DYNASTIES WITHIN ORGANIZATIONS: WHEN POSITION BECOMES A PRIVILEGE FOR THE INNER CIRCLE

Professional organizations should be built on competence, meritocracy, and equal opportunity — not gradually transformed into networks of privilege based on family ties and personal connections.

There is an issue worth examining within professional organizations.

A company may have established recruitment policies, promotion procedures, career development frameworks, and competency standards designed to ensure fairness and equal opportunities for everyone.

But what happens when individuals holding senior positions use their authority and influence to bring their children, relatives, or close associates into the organization — sometimes placing them directly into senior management or strategic positions?

This raises concerns that go far beyond ordinary recruitment decisions.

It touches on leadership integrity, conflicts of interest, corporate governance, and organizational justice.

A Position of Authority Is Not a License to Build a Personal Power Network

Every leadership position comes with authority. However, that authority exists to serve the interests of the organization, not the personal interests of the individual holding it or their family.

When authority is used to provide privileged access to people within a leader's personal circle, while other employees must go through lengthy selection processes, competency assessments, and established career paths, questions about organizational fairness inevitably arise.

Do the same rules apply to everyone?

Or does a separate pathway exist for those who have personal connections with people in power?

Being Competent Does Not Automatically Make the Process Fair

We should approach this issue objectively.

Not everyone who has family ties with a senior executive is necessarily unqualified. They may possess the education, experience, and capabilities required for the position.

However, individual competence does not automatically justify the process through which someone is appointed.

Research by Burhan, van Leeuwen, and Scheepers (2020), involving five experiments conducted in Indonesia and the United States, found that hiring relatives was perceived as nepotism regardless of their competence. The research also highlighted concerns about procedural fairness and the potential difficulty of attracting qualified applicants. [1]

If someone is placed directly into a senior position, several questions deserve to be asked:

* Was the recruitment or appointment process transparent?
* Were other qualified candidates given equal consideration?
* Were the position requirements consistently applied?
* Was the appointment subject to independent review and appropriate governance  procedures?

In a well-governed organization, it is not only the final decision that matters. The process behind that decision must also be fair, transparent, and accountable.

The Consequences Extend Beyond Individual Employees

Such practices can create broader organizational risks.

1. Erosion of Meritocracy
Employees may begin to question whether performance, competence, and experience still determine career advancement.

2. Declining Motivation and Leadership Succession
Talented internal employees may lose confidence in their career prospects when they perceive that opportunities are influenced more by personal connections than professional achievements.

3. The Formation of Closed Power Networks
When strategic positions are increasingly occupied by individuals connected to the same circle of influence, organizational independence and effective oversight may become vulnerable.

4. Risks to Leadership Quality
Organizations may miss the opportunity to appoint the most suitable candidates because decisions are influenced by personal relationships rather than organizational needs and professional qualifications.

A 2025 study by Pagano and Picariello in Review of Finance examines how corporate governance influences merit-based hiring and promotion. Their research highlights how the private benefits of retaining control can create incentives for non-meritocratic promotion practices, potentially at the expense of organizational efficiency. [2]

A Professional Organization Is Not a Platform for Building Personal Dynasties

An organization exists to achieve collective objectives, not to serve as an instrument for expanding the personal influence of its leaders.

Children, relatives, and close associates have the same right as anyone else to pursue employment and build their careers.

But they should also be subject to the same standards, requirements, and selection processes.

There should be no privileged route simply because someone has a personal relationship with a senior executive.

A 2025 integrative review by Schilpzand, Lagios, and Restubog in Human Resource Management examines nepotism from the perspectives of those who initiate it, those who benefit from it, and other employees affected by it. It also discusses evidence-based approaches to recruitment, promotion, evaluation, and compensation involving relatives. [3]

If organizational rules are strictly enforced for ordinary employees but become flexible when members of the inner circle are involved, then the issue is no longer merely about individual behavior.

It raises a fundamental question about the integrity of the organization's governance system.

A Reflection for Those in Positions of Power

When you are entrusted with a leadership position, you are given the responsibility to manage and develop an organization.

It is not an opportunity to build a family power network.

Nor is it an opportunity to create an inner circle with privileged access to positions, influence, and decision-making authority.

True leadership should leave behind a stronger system, not an organization dependent on the personal networks of those who once held power.

Ultimately, a leader's legacy should not be measured by how many relatives or close associates have secured strategic positions.

It should be measured by how fair the system has become, how many talents have been developed, and how strong the organization remains after that leader has left office.

Do not use your position to build a dynasty. Use your authority to build an organization where everyone has a fair opportunity to succeed.

References & Further Reading

[1] Burhan, O. K., van Leeuwen, E., & Scheepers, D. (2020).
On the hiring of kin in organizations: Perceived nepotism and its implications for fairness perceptions and the willingness to join an organization.
Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, 161, 34–48.

Corporate governance, meritocracy, and careers.

Who owns the know-how after the visiting engineers leave?

For manufacturers entering or expanding in Indonesia, technology transfer is also a recruitment decision.

Language fluency helps teams communicate. It does not, by itself, demonstrate process ownership, quality judgment or the ability to train others.

Before recruiting your Indonesia team, align Operations and HR around three questions:
Ownership: Which process, quality decision or training outcome will this person own?
Evidence: What comparable experience shows they can absorb, apply and explain new methods?
Readiness: How will you assess whether the team can perform after the handover?
Turn those answers into role requirements—not just a list of qualifications.

For engineering, quality and production leadership roles, use structured interviews and fictional work scenarios. Ask candidates how they would diagnose a process issue, document learning and validate team readiness. Avoid requesting confidential materials from previous employers.

Map the talent early. Align hiring dates with approved project milestones.

posts.text:
The calendar said 17:30. That's 23:30 where I sit.

I run Kogentic from Jakarta, with a small remote team and developers we're learning from across Europe and the US. A developer just booked a user interview on our European calendar. The slot looked civilised: 17:30. Then I did the conversion. 11:30 for the person joining from the US. 23:30 for me. Nobody did anything wrong. The time was right for them. It just wasn't evening for all three of us.

I said yes anyway. I'll be on the call, and I asked an AI notetaker to join as backup. Not to run it. Just so the notes don't depend on how sharp I am at 23:30. We're building software for developers who work like this — across time zones, with AI in the loop — and it would be a bit rich to preach that and then dodge the late one.

The lesson I keep relearning: a calendar time is always someone's local time, and rarely everyone's. The work is deciding whose clock you're willing to honour, and how you still show up when it's yours that loses. What's the latest call you've taken because the other person's 17:30 wasn't yours?

A message queue stores messages until they're consumed, but the Jakarta Messaging standard deliberately leaves some behavior undefined, including how long a queue keeps messages and what happens when resources overflow. Worth knowing before you rely on it.

#MessageQueue #Messaging #DistributedSystems #Constraints #SystemDesign #SoftwareEngineering #BackendDevelopment #Reliability #Architecture #Developers #TechCommunity #LessonsLearned

More info
• Expiration has limits. An undelivered message that reaches its expiration time should be destroyed, and clients shouldn't receive expired messages. But the standard doesn't guarantee they won't, and it defines no notification when a message expires.

• Priority is best effort too. There are ten levels, 0 to 9, with 0 to 4 as normal and 5 to 9 as expedited. A provider doesn't have to enforce strict priority ordering; it only has to do its best to deliver expedited messages ahead of normal ones. #JakartaMessaging #Priority
